YOUR POOL (approved)

Four things, in order. Tap any picture to see it full size.

1. The plan: your pool area as it is today

2. The 3D: your p02 design on your real plan

What all four of your images share, now on your pool: a closed bamboo backdrop behind the garden (no glass fence through the middle), one focal cloud tree at the end of the pool with lanterns either side (p01), loungers on pebbles flowing straight off the timber (p02), natural pale grey rocks. Then p02 detail by detail:

  • A clean rectangle: the step-out corner at the gym end is filled in and decked over, so every edge is one straight line, and the glass fence on the house side runs in one straight line too.
  • Timber all the way round: the rock garden pulls back to the house wing, so the dark timber runs across the west end of the pool and joins the house-side deck to the view deck.
  • A moss garden with rocks in the empty timber triangle past the pool glass: moss-look cushion plants in a tray set into the deck, three pale grey rocks.
  • The wide stepped slate platform: four broad slate terraces stepping down from the straight edge at the gym end (a new concrete step platform on the pool floor, slate-clad).
  • Clear dark water with the slate tiles and steps showing through.
  • The lily pads beside the steps: tethered artificial floating pads with a few pink flowers (real lilies die in pool water).
  • Narrow dark timber right to the water: 94 mm boards in DecoWood Dark Mocha; every edge straight, every corner square.
  • Two white loungers angled to the water on low sled-shaped timber frames, the low table with a bowl between them, the dark tray with a teapot by the water, two round white floor poufs.
  • The pebble bed: blue-black river stones with irregular pale flat stones, two white loungers, a pale rock.
  • The twisted silver tree: cloud-pruned olives (silver trunk, grey-green pads), one behind the loungers on a moss mound, one on the rock island.
  • The bamboo wall: a 1.8 m bamboo-look fence (round bamboo-coloured aluminium poles, fireproof) along the whole neighbour boundary. It is the pool fence there too, so the glass between the pool deck and the lounger garden is gone. Live bamboo clumps in front of it.
  • p01’s end view: the same bamboo fence behind the olive at the end of the pool, with a glowing lantern either side (a real black square LED bollard, 600 mm tall; a true Japanese box lantern like p01’s would be custom-made, about $500–700 each).
  • One garden along the bamboo: pebbles, pale stones and loungers, then moss and pale rocks, the olive, bamboo clumps and a lantern.
  • Not copied: the stone edge (you chose all wood), the hut (that is your gym), and a 6 m bamboo wall (the bushfire rules keep live bamboo to about 2 m near the gym glass).

INSIDE: the Komatsu look, no white walls

Like your Komatsu photo: the contrast is a dark charcoal stone floor against a pale grey split-face stone wall in long, rough courses, with white walls and warm timber around them. The floor is honed bluestone tiles, 600 × 400, through the whole living area upstairs and down. The one stone wall is the garage wall under the mezzanine, behind the stairs. Pale timber stays on the stairs, the front-door landing, the raised bench and the mezzanine.

Why every hard floor is dear here: the living floor is timber-framed, so stone, porcelain and microcement all need the boards up, the joists stiffened and fibre-cement sheet laid first, and every price carries the contingency and builder’s margin. Porcelain is cheaper than microcement, but both are far dearer than staining the timber you already have, the dark timber floor of your Komatsu photo k3. Test-stain an old and a new board first (spotted gum takes stain unevenly; a black-tinted hardwax oil gives the most even near-black).

The earlier tile options (not chosen)

Your pick: concrete-look hybrid tiles, the cheapest way to the cement look. Product: Aries SPC hybrid (Ross’s Discount Home Centre), a pale grey stone/concrete blend with warm and cool grey flecks, 615 × 311 mm tiles, 6.5 mm with the underlay built in, about $80 a box. Laid half-bond with fine bevelled joints, upstairs and down; the little landing at the top of the stair stays timber. In the 3D now; the real render is being made.

Price: microcement is dearer, not cheaper. Whole house (263 m², upstairs and down), all-in, against the floors the plan already carries ($9,100–20,700):

FloorAll-inExtra over the plan
Microcement (truly seamless)$93,300–138,700+$84,200–118,000
Cement-look porcelain tiles 1200×600, 2 mm matching grout (near seamless, never needs resealing)$70,600–113,600+$61,600–92,900
Concrete-look hybrid planks (the cheapest way to the look; a joint every 0.3–0.6 m)$30,100–67,200+$21,000–46,500

Why microcement costs so much here: your upstairs floor is suspended timber, so the boards have to come up, the bouncy joists be stiffened and cement sheet laid before the microcement; downstairs is a slab, but the glued timber has to come up first and the slab has a crack and damp at the east wall, so it needs a 10–20 mm overlay. Cheapest smart way: the concrete-look hybrid planks in a pale shade.

Side by side: hybrid tiles vs porcelain tiles

Left: concrete-look hybrid (Aries SPC, 615 × 311, joints every 0.3–0.6 m), whole house about $30,100–67,200 all-in. Right: cement-look porcelain (Tilemall Arcadia 1200 × 600, stack bond, 2 mm grout matched to the tile, so the joints almost vanish; never needs resealing), about $70,600–113,600. Porcelain needs the upstairs boards up, the joists stiffened and cement sheet laid first; the hybrid floats on top. Real renders of both are being made.

INSIDE: the upstairs kitchen becomes one big window with a bench (approved)

What you asked: take out the upstairs kitchen, one big glass panel the same size, raise the floor inside to make a bench, make it like the Komatsu house. In the 3D now:

  • The kitchenette is gone: bench and sink, the tall oak cupboard, the island, the stools. Your main kitchen stays downstairs.
  • One big pane: the front wall where the kitchen was becomes a single 4.2 × 2.24 m pane in a slim black steel frame. The side wall by the front door stays as it is.
  • The raised bench: the floor along the glass rises into a pale timber bench, 450 mm high and 850 mm deep, the full 4 m width, slatted top, a black shadow line at the floor, a grey linen pad. It stops short of the bathroom door.

  • Price: about $93,100 all-in (Flame Zone, incl. GST, contingency and margin): the big pane with its fire shutter about $63,400, the bench about $5,300, the timber ceiling and joists about $3,500, the moss garden about $3,000, strip-out, the steel beam, engineer and making good about $17,900.
  • To know: no fire-tested Flame Zone glass comes in one pane this big (they stop at about 2.4 m on a side), so the pane is fireproof-rated BAL-40 double glazing behind a stainless fire roller shutter that rolls down only in a bushfire; its box hides in the wall above the glass, with slim guide channels each side. The pane weighs about 280 kg, so it goes in by crane. If your bushfire report rates that street wall BAL-40 instead of Flame Zone, the shutter is not needed and the price drops by about $34,000.

What Flame Zone rules out, plainly: bamboo (dense clumps that hold dead leaves next to the house fail the bushfire planting rules) and black pine or juniper (resinous, they burn hot), so the cloud tree is a cloud-pruned Podocarpus, which looks the same. Waterlilies can’t live in a pool. A dark tiled interior like p01/p02 would add $22,800–50,700, so the charcoal quartz is used.

Swaps that fit: chunkier 60 mm drop-face coping like p02, +$2,959. A real carved granite lantern, +$1,367.

Check now: the 2022 drawings say “POOL HAS NO FENCE”. If the house came with a pool certificate of non-compliance, NSW gives 90 days from settlement to fix it. Nothing here has been measured on site or quoted yet.

Ideas boards

The look for both designs: dark charred timber outside, corrugated steel roofs, slim black glass, warm timber ceilings and soffits running out past the glass, cement-look floors, a concrete cone fireplace and a curved sofa.

The roof: four bold ideas, all real built houses

Same roof shapes as today. Each idea uses real materials that are safe in a flame zone. Pick one or mix them.

1. One dark block

Roof and walls in one dark metal skin, folded crisply at the edges, so each of today's roof forms reads as a single dark block with the glass cut in, like the Komatsu boxes. Same roof shapes; steel, aluminium and zinc are metal and don't burn, so they suit the flame zone.

2. Dark zinc

The same roof shapes in factory-weathered dark zinc instead of painted steel, which gives a soft stone-like sheen, finer seams and crisp folded edges that can carry on down the walls. Zinc is metal and doesn't burn (Glenn Murcutt chose it at Palm Beach partly for the bushfire risk), but it costs more than Colorbond.

3. Black steel rafters outside

Slim black steel rafters run out past the glass so the eaves show their structure, like the Komatsu ceiling of timber joists on black steel carried on outside. Same roof shapes; the rafters would be steel, not timber, because steel doesn't burn.

4. A veil of vertical fins

Tall slender fins stand just off the walls and fill the gable ends, screening the glass like the blades on Komatsu's house, with the roof shapes unchanged. In the flame zone they would be black steel or timber-look aluminium rather than real timber, since metal doesn't burn.

The roof: a dark lid over the glass (first photos: the safe version)

Same roof shapes as today. Smooth dark charcoal metal (Colorbond Monument), thin black edges, timber-look battens under the eaves. Real products, sold in Sydney.

The house you love: Hayato Komatsu Architects' own house, Hiroshima

Photos via home-designing.com. What we take from it: exposed timber rafters on black steel beams, black steel glass on two sides, a garden pressed against the glass, dark stone walls, a slatted timber floor and black mesh balustrade at the stair void, a red rug.

Your favourites (8 Nov): the direction

What runs through them: a Japanese-style bush house. Dark charred timber outside, pale timber ceilings and exposed rafters inside, cement floors, a courtyard with one tree, boulders and ferns, glass that opens whole walls to the garden, an open timber stair, and one bold curved sofa.

D+: pitched roofs kept, dark timber pavilion, tall timber ceiling inside

C with the courtyard: one roof lifting to the view, a bush courtyard cut into the house

    Decision 1 · the roof

    Low at the front, rising to the view

    Both options rise from front to back, never left to right, and both stop at RL 114.55 at the view glass, 50 mm under the 8.5 m height line measured from the pool paving below. Today's ridge (RL 115.99) sits over the front of the house, where the ground is 3 m higher; the same RL at the rear would be 9.6 m above the ground there, so it is not allowed. A flat strip over the stair bay keeps 2.2 m over S2 and the mezzanine edge. The options differ in where the slope starts.

    Recommended · Option C

    One roof plane from today's front gutter, capped under the height line

    Option B

    Keep the low front roof, start the new roof behind it

    Option C is your first description: the roof starts low at the entrance, as it does now, and climbs in one plane to the glass. The ceiling goes from 2.7 m at the front of the living room to 4.6 m at the glass. Option B keeps the low roof you see from the driveway and starts the new roof where it ends, so the climb is gentler and the front of the room is 3.3 m. In both, the 2.1 m wide strip over S2 and the mezzanine edge stays flat at RL 114.55, the height of the eave of the roof kept over the garage, so S2 stays where it is and the mezzanine stays open to the room.
